Chapter Six
第六章
About this time an ambitious young reporter from New York arrived one morning at Gatsby’s door and asked him if he had anything to say.
差不多就是那时候，一天早晨，一个急于出头的纽约年轻记者来到盖茨比门口，问他有没有什么话要说。
“Anything to say about what?” inquired Gatsby politely.
“关于什么的话？”盖茨比客气地问。
“Why—any statement to give out.”
“呃……就是，有没有什么声明要发表。”
It transpired after a confused five minutes that the man had heard Gatsby’s name around his office in a connection
经过五分钟的混乱之后，人们发现那个男人曾在办公室里听到过盖茨比的名字。
which he either wouldn’t reveal or didn’t fully understand.
他要么不会透露这些事情，要么根本就不完全理解它们。
This was his day off and with laudable initiative he had hurried out “to see.”
这是他的休息日，出于值得称赞的主动精神，他匆忙地出门去“看看”。
It was a random shot, and yet the reporter’s instinct was right.
那是一记随机的射击，但记者的直觉是正确的。
Gatsby’s notoriety, spread about by the hundreds who had accepted his hospitality
好几百人受过盖茨比的款待，
and so become authorities upon his past, had increased all summer until he fell just short of being news.
也就自命是他的身世专家。他的名声让这些人传得越来越响，一个夏天下来，简直快成新闻人物了。
Contemporary legends such as the “underground pipeline to Canada” attached themselves to him, and there was one persistent story
当代的传说，比如“通往加拿大的地下通道”这样的故事，都附在他身上。还有一个流传已久的故事……
that he didn’t live in a house at all, but in a boat
他根本不住在房子里，而是住在船上。
that looked like a house and was moved secretly up and down the Long Island shore.
那栋建筑看起来就像一座房子，它被秘密地安置在长岛的海岸上。
Just why these inventions were a source of satisfaction to James Gatz of North Dakota, isn’t easy to say.
很难说，这些发明究竟为何能让北达科他州的詹姆斯·盖茨感到满足。
James Gatz—that was really, or at least legally, his name.
詹姆斯·盖茨——那确实是他的名字，或者至少从法律上讲，是他的名字。
He had changed it at the age of seventeen and at the specific moment
他十七岁时就改变了这个名字，而那个特定的时刻……
that witnessed the beginning of his career—when he saw Dan Cody’s yacht drop anchor over the most insidious flat on Lake Superior.
那场事件标志着他职业生涯的起点——当时，他看到丹·科迪的游艇在苏必利尔湖上那片平坦的水面上抛锚。
It was James Gatz who had been loafing along the beach that afternoon in a torn green jersey
那天下午，在沙滩上闲逛的，正是詹姆斯·盖茨，他穿着一件破旧的绿色运动衫。
and a pair of canvas pants, but it was already Jay Gatsby who borrowed a rowboat,
还有一条帆布裤子，不过当时借船的，还是杰伊·盖茨比。
pulled out to the Tuolomee, and informed Cody that a wind might catch him and break him up in half an hour.
他划船来到托洛梅河边，并告诉科迪，一阵风可能会把他吹倒，他可能在半小时内就会断气。
I suppose he’d had the name ready for a long time, even then.
我想，他早就想好这个名字了，甚至从很久以前就开始构思了。
His parents were shiftless and unsuccessful farm people—his imagination had never really accepted them as his parents at all.
他的父母都是些不务正业、经营不善的农场主——他的想象力根本无法真正接受他们作为自己的父母这一事实。
The truth was that Jay Gatsby of West Egg, Long Island, sprang from his Platonic conception of himself.
事实上，来自长岛西卵的杰伊·盖茨比，源自他自我认知中的理想化形象。
He was a son of God—a phrase which, if it means anything, means just that—
他是个上帝之子——这句话，如果它真的有什么意义的话，那就只是意味着如此而已。
and he must be about His Father’s business, the service of a vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.
他肯定是在处理与父亲相关的事务——也就是为一位庞大、庸俗且只追求感官享受的美女服务。
So he invented just the sort of Jay Gatsby that a seventeen-year-old boy would be likely to invent,
于是，他创造出了一个典型的杰伊·盖茨比形象——一个十七岁的男孩可能会想象出的那种形象。
and to this conception he was faithful to the end.
他一直忠实于这个形象，直到最后。
For over a year he had been beating his way along the south shore of Lake Superior as a clam-digger
一年多的时间里，他一直沿着苏必利尔湖的南岸，以采蛤为生。
and a salmon-fisher or in any other capacity that brought him food and bed.
还有一位鲑鱼捕捞者，或者任何能为他提供食物和住所的人。
His brown, hardening body lived naturally through the half-fierce, half-lazy work of the bracing days.
他那棕色的、逐渐变硬的身躯，是在那些充满活力的日子里，通过半是忙碌、半是懒散的生活状态而自然形成的。
He knew women early, and since they spoiled him he became contemptuous of them, of young virgins
他早早地认识了许多女性，但由于她们让他感到厌烦，因此他对她们，尤其是对那些年轻处女，都充满了轻蔑之情。
because they were ignorant, of the others because they were hysterical about things which in his overwhelming self-absorption he took for granted.
因为他们无知，对其他人则充满狂热的态度；而他，由于极度自我中心，认为这些事情都是理所当然的。
But his heart was in a constant, turbulent riot.
但他的内心却处于一种持续而动荡的混乱状态。
The most grotesque and fantastic conceits haunted him in his bed at night.
那些最怪异、最奇幻的幻想在夜晚的床上缠绕着他。
A universe of ineffable gaudiness spun itself out in his brain while the clock ticked on the washstand
在那个洗漱台旁，时钟滴答作响，而他的脑海中却盘旋着无数难以言喻的华丽幻想。
and the moon soaked with wet light his tangled clothes upon the floor.
月亮洒下湿润的光芒，照亮了地板上那些凌乱的衣物。
Each night he added to the pattern of his fancies until drowsiness closed down upon some vivid scene with an oblivious embrace.
每个夜晚，他都会不断为自己的幻想增添新的元素，直到昏昏欲睡之际，那些生动的场景与无意识的拥抱融为一体。
For a while these reveries provided an outlet for his imagination; they were a satisfactory hint of the unreality of reality,
在一段时间内，这些幻想为他的想象力提供了宣泄的渠道；它们是对现实非真实性的一种令人满意的描述。
a promise that the rock of the world was founded securely on a fairy’s wing.
一个承诺，即世界的基石是建立在仙女之翼之上的。
An instinct toward his future glory had led him, some months before, to the small Lutheran College of St. Olaf’s in southern Minnesota.
几个月前，一种对未来的荣耀的直觉促使他来到了明尼苏达州南部的小圣奥拉夫路德教会学院。
He stayed there two weeks, dismayed at its ferocious indifference to the drums of his destiny,
他只在那里待了两个星期。关乎他命运的鼓声那么响，那地方却冷漠得近乎残酷，叫他大感沮丧。
to destiny itself, and despising the janitor’s work with which he was to pay his way through.
它对命运本身也同样无动于衷。而要靠做校工来挣学费，又是他不屑做的事。
Then he drifted back to Lake Superior, and he was still searching for something to do on the day
然后，他回到了苏必利尔湖。那天，他仍在寻找自己能做的事情。
that Dan Cody’s yacht dropped anchor in the shallows alongshore.
丹·科迪的游艇在岸边较浅的水域抛锚了。
Cody was fifty years old then, a product of the Nevada silver fields, of the Yukon, of every rush for metal since seventy-five.
那时，科迪已经五十岁了。他是内华达州银矿区的产物，也是育空地区的人。自19世纪75年代以来，他一直致力于金属资源的开发工作。
The transactions in Montana copper that made him many times a millionaire found him physically robust
那些在蒙大拿州铜矿中进行的交易让他成为了百万富翁，他的身体也变得非常健壮。
but on the verge of soft-mindedness, and, suspecting this, an infinite number of women tried to separate him from his money.
但在他即将走向软弱无力的边缘时，无数女性都试图把他与他的财富分离开来。
The none too savoury ramifications by which Ella Kaye, the newspaper woman, played Madame de Maintenon to his weakness
那位报社女记者艾拉·凯，以其那略带讽刺的举止，成功地扮演了玛德琳·德·马纳顿这一角色，从而加剧了他的弱点。
and sent him to sea in a yacht, were common property of the turgid journalism in 1902.
他被送到海上去，乘坐一艘游艇。在1902年，这种行为被认为是普通的新闻报道中的常见现象。
He had been coasting along all too hospitable shores for five years when he turned up as James Gatz’s destiny in Little Girl Bay.
在那些过于友善的海岸线上度过了五年时光后，他最终以詹姆斯·盖茨的身份出现在小女孩湾。
To young Gatz, resting on his oars and looking up at the railed deck, that yacht represented all the beauty and glamour in the world.
对于年轻的盖茨来说，当他躺在桨上，仰望甲板上的天空时，那艘游艇仿佛代表了世界上所有的美丽与魅力。
I suppose he smiled at Cody—he had probably discovered that people liked him when he smiled.
我想，他微笑着对科迪说道——也许他发现自己之所以受欢迎，正是因为他的微笑。
At any rate Cody asked him a few questions (one of them elicited the brand new name) and found that he was quick and extravagantly ambitious.
无论如何，科迪向他问了几个问题（其中一个问题引出了那个全新的名字），结果发现他非常敏捷且野心勃勃。
A few days later he took him to Duluth and bought him a blue coat, six pairs of white duck trousers, and a yachting cap.
几天后，他带他去杜鲁斯，给他买了一件蓝色外套、六条白色的鸭布裤子，还有一顶航海帽。
And when the Tuolomee left for the West Indies and the Barbary Coast, Gatsby left too.
当图奥洛米离开前往西印度群岛和巴巴里海岸时，盖茨比也离开了。
He was employed in a vague personal capacity—while he remained with Cody he was in turn steward,
他以一种模糊的私人身份从事这项工作——尽管他一直与科迪在一起，但他实际上还是担任着管理职务。
mate, skipper, secretary, and even jailor, for Dan Cody sober knew what lavish doings Dan Cody drunk might soon be about,
伴侣、船长、秘书，甚至还有监狱长——因为丹·科迪很清楚，那些奢华的聚会很快就会开始，而丹·科迪很快就会沉醉其中。
and he provided for such contingencies by reposing more and more trust in Gatsby.
他通过逐渐增加对盖茨比的信任，为这种可能性做好了准备。
The arrangement lasted five years, during which the boat went three times around the Continent.
这段关系持续了五年，期间那艘船三次环游了欧洲大陆。
It might have lasted indefinitely except for the fact
这样的日子本来兴许会一直过下去，偏偏
that Ella Kaye came on board one night in Boston and a week later Dan Cody inhospitably died.
在波士顿的一个晚上，埃拉·凯上了船。一个星期后，丹·科迪竟怠慢客人似的死了。
I remember the portrait of him up in Gatsby’s bedroom, a grey, florid man with a hard,
我记得他在盖茨比卧室里的画像，那是一个面容憔悴、容光焕发的男人，眼神坚定而冷漠。
empty face—the pioneer debauchee, who during one phase of American life brought back to the Eastern seaboard the savage violence of the frontier brothel and saloon.
空洞的面容——那个在美洲生活的一个阶段中，将边疆妓院和酒馆中的野蛮暴力带回到东海岸的狂妄之徒。
It was indirectly due to Cody that Gatsby drank so little.
之所以盖茨比很少饮酒，间接也是因为科迪的缘故。
Sometimes in the course of gay parties women used to rub champagne into his hair; for himself he formed the habit of letting liquor alone.
有时候，在那些同性恋派对上，女性们会把香槟涂抹在他的头发上；而他自己则更喜欢只喝烈酒。
And it was from Cody that he inherited money—a legacy of twenty-five thousand dollars.
而这笔钱，就是他从科迪那里继承来的——一笔价值两万五千美元的遗产。
He didn’t get it.
他并不明白这一点。
He never understood the legal device that was used against him, but what remained of the millions went intact to Ella Kaye.
他始终无法理解那些用来对付他的法律手段，但那数百万美元的财产却完好无损地落入了埃拉·凯的手中。
He was left with his singularly appropriate education; the vague contour of Jay Gatsby had filled out to the substantiality of a man.
他只接受了有限的教育；杰伊那模糊的轮廓已经变得像一个真正的男人一样健壮。
He told me all this very much later,
他后来才告诉我这一切。
but I’ve put it down here with the idea of exploding those first wild rumours about his antecedents, which weren’t even faintly true.
不过，我把这些话写下来，是为了揭露那些关于他出身的荒谬传闻，那些传闻根本就不真实。
Moreover he told it to me at a time of confusion, when I had reached the point of believing everything and nothing about him.
此外，他是在我陷入困惑的时候向我讲述这些事情的，当时我对他的所有事情都抱有一概而知的幻想，但实际上这些说法根本并不真实。
So I take advantage of this short halt, while Gatsby, so to speak, caught his breath, to clear this set of misconceptions away.
因此，我趁这个短暂的停顿时机，试图消除这些误解。可以说，当时我正处于一种困惑的状态，对盖茨比的一切都抱有一分或三分怀疑的态度。而此时，他与他的事务之间的关联也暂时中断了。
It was a halt, too, in my association with his affairs.
这也是我与他的事务关系中断的一个阶段。
For several weeks I didn’t see him or hear his voice on the phone—mostly I was in New York,
有几周的时间，我既没见过他，也听不到他在电话里的声音——大部分时间我都在纽约。
trotting around with Jordan and trying to ingratiate myself with her senile aunt—but finally I went over to his house one Sunday afternoon.
我试图与乔丹混在一起，试图赢得她那位老糊涂阿姨的青睐——但最终，在一个星期天的下午，我还是去了他的家。
I hadn’t been there two minutes when somebody brought Tom Buchanan in for a drink.
我刚到那里不到两分钟，就有人带着汤姆·布坎南来请他喝一杯。
I was startled, naturally, but the really surprising thing was that it hadn’t happened before.
当然，我感到很惊讶，但真正令人惊讶的是，这种事情以前从未发生过过。
They were a party of three on horseback—Tom and a man named Sloane and a pretty woman in a brown riding-habit, who had been there previously.
他们是一组三人，骑着马出行——汤姆、一个名叫斯隆的男人，还有一个穿着棕色马术服的漂亮女人。那个女人之前也来过这里。
“I’m delighted to see you,” said Gatsby, standing on his porch.
“我很高兴见到你，”盖茨比站在他的门廊上说道。
“I’m delighted that you dropped in.”
“你们能顺路过来，我真高兴。”
As though they cared!
好像他们真的在乎似的！
“Sit right down. Have a cigarette or a cigar.”
“请坐下来吧。可以抽根烟或者雪茄。”
He walked around the room quickly, ringing bells.
他快速地在房间里走动，手机铃声响个不停。
“I’ll have something to drink for you in just a minute.”
“我马上就会为您准备一些饮料。”
He was profoundly affected by the fact that Tom was there.
汤姆的在场让他深受感动。
But he would be uneasy anyhow until he had given them something, realizing in a vague way that that was all they came for.
但无论如何，他会感到不安，直到他能够给他们一些东西。他隐约意识到，他们来这里的目的其实就是为了这些。
Mr. Sloane wanted nothing.
斯隆先生什么也不想要。
A lemonade?
柠檬水？
No, thanks.
不用了，谢谢。
A little champagne?
一点香槟？
Nothing at all, thanks … I’m sorry—
没什么，谢谢……很抱歉——
“Did you have a nice ride?”
“这次的旅程很愉快吧？”
“Very good roads around here.”
“这里的道路非常好。”
“I suppose the automobiles—”
“我想，那些汽车……”
“Yeah.”
“是的。”
Moved by an irresistible impulse, Gatsby turned to Tom, who had accepted the introduction as a stranger.
被一种难以抗拒的冲动所驱使，盖茨比转向了汤姆，汤姆已经接受了这个陌生人的介绍。
“I believe we’ve met somewhere before, Mr. Buchanan.”
“我相信我们之前在某个地方见过面，布坎南先生。”
“Oh, yes,” said Tom, gruffly polite, but obviously not remembering.
“哦，是的，”汤姆客气而粗哑地回答，但显然他不记得之前是否见过对方了。
“So we did. I remember very well.”
“我们确实这么做了。我记忆非常清晰。”
“About two weeks ago.”
“大约两周前。”
“That’s right. You were with Nick here.”
“没错。你当时和尼克在一起。”
“I know your wife,” continued Gatsby, almost aggressively.
“我认识你的妻子，”盖茨比继续说道，语气中带着一丝敌意。
“That so?”
“是吗？”
Tom turned to me.
汤姆转向我。
“You live near here, Nick?”
“你住在这里附近吗，尼克？”
“Next door.”
“隔壁。”
“That so?”
“是吗？”
Mr. Sloane didn’t enter into the conversation, but lounged back haughtily in his chair; the woman said nothing either—until unexpectedly, after two highballs, she became cordial.
斯隆先生没有参与对话，只是傲慢地坐在椅子上；那个女人也没有说话——直到两杯威士忌下肚后，她突然变得友善起来。
“We’ll all come over to your next party, Mr. Gatsby,” she suggested.
“我们都会参加你的下一次派对，盖茨比先生，”她提议道。
“What do you say?”
“您意下如何？”
“Certainly; I’d be delighted to have you.”
“当然可以；我很乐意邀请您。”
“Be ver’ nice,” said Mr. Sloane, without gratitude.
“请务必友善一些吧，”斯隆先生说，语气中并无感激之情。
“Well—think ought to be starting home.”
“嗯——我觉得应该先回家吧。”
“Please don’t hurry,” Gatsby urged them.
“请不要着急，”盖茨比恳求他们。
He had control of himself now, and he wanted to see more of Tom.
现在，他能够控制自己的情绪了，而且他希望更多地见到汤姆。
“Why don’t you—why don’t you stay for supper? I wouldn’t be surprised if some other people dropped in from New York.”
“你为什么不住下来共进晚餐呢？如果还有其他人从纽约过来，我也不会感到惊讶。”
“You come to supper with me,” said the lady enthusiastically.
“你愿意和我一起共进晚餐吗？”那位女士热情地说道。
“Both of you.”
“你们两个。”
This included me.
这其中包括我。
Mr. Sloane got to his feet.
斯隆先生站了起来。
“Come along,” he said—but to her only.
“请过来吧，”他说——但那只是对她说的。
“I mean it,” she insisted.
“我是认真的，”她坚持说道。
“I’d love to have you. Lots of room.”
“我很希望你能加入我们。这里有很多空间。”
Gatsby looked at me questioningly.
盖茨比用疑惑的眼神看着我。
He wanted to go and he didn’t see that Mr. Sloane had determined he shouldn’t.
他想要去，但他没有意识到斯隆先生已经决定不允许他这么做。
“I’m afraid I won’t be able to,” I said.
“恐怕我无法去了，”我说。
“Well, you come,” she urged, concentrating on Gatsby.
“好吧，你还是来吧，”她催促道，同时全神贯注地盯着盖茨比。
Mr. Sloane murmured something close to her ear.
斯隆先生在她耳边低声说了些什么。
“We won’t be late if we start now,” she insisted aloud.
“如果我们现在开始的话，就不会迟到，”她大声坚持说道。
“I haven’t got a horse,” said Gatsby.
“我没有马了，”盖茨比说。
“I used to ride in the army,
“我以前在军队里当过兵。”
but I’ve never bought a horse. I’ll have to follow you in my car. Excuse me for just a minute.”
不过，我从未养过马。我只能坐车跟着你走了。请稍等片刻，我这就离开一下。
The rest of us walked out on the porch, where Sloane and the lady began an impassioned conversation aside.
其余的人则走到门廊上，斯隆和那位女士在旁边开始了一场热烈的交谈。
“My God, I believe the man’s coming,” said Tom.
“我的天啊，我觉得那个男人会来吧，”汤姆说道。
“Doesn’t he know she doesn’t want him?”
“他难道不知道她并不想要他吗？”
“She says she does want him.”
“她说她确实想要他。”
“She has a big dinner party and he won’t know a soul there.”

“You can’t repeat the past.”
“过去的事没法重来。”
“Can’t repeat the past?” he cried incredulously.
“过去的事没法重来？”他喊了起来，简直不敢相信。
“Why of course you can!”
“怎么会？当然能！”
He looked around him wildly, as if the past were lurking here in the shadow of his house, just out of reach of his hand.
他慌乱地环顾四周，仿佛往日就躲在他家宅子的阴影里，只差一点便能伸手够着。
“I’m going to fix everything just the way it was before,” he said, nodding determinedly.
“我会把一切都安排得跟从前一模一样。”他说着，坚决地点了点头。
“She’ll see.”
“她会明白的。”
He talked a lot about the past, and I gathered
他谈起了许多往事。我渐渐听明白了，
that he wanted to recover something, some idea of himself perhaps, that had gone into loving Daisy.
他想找回某样东西，也许是当年爱上黛西时，他寄托在那份爱里的一种自我想象。
His life had been confused and disordered since then, but if he could once return to a certain starting place
从那以后，他的生活便乱了套。不过，只要能回到某个起点，
and go over it all slowly, he could find out what that thing was …
把一切慢慢重走一遍，他就能弄清那究竟是什么……
… One autumn night, five years before, they had been walking down the street when the leaves were falling,
……五年前一个秋夜，他们走在落叶纷飞的街上，
and they came to a place where there were no trees and the sidewalk was white with moonlight.
来到一处没有树的地方，月光把人行道照得雪白。
They stopped here and turned toward each other.
他们停下脚步，转过身来，面对着面。
Now it was a cool night with that mysterious excitement in it which comes at the two changes of the year.
那是一个清凉的夜晚，透着一种神秘的悸动，一年里只有春秋换季时才有。
The quiet lights in the houses were humming out into the darkness and there was a stir and bustle among the stars.
屋里安静的灯光仿佛嗡嗡低鸣，一直传到黑暗中去；天上的星星间也一阵骚动。
Out of the corner of his eye Gatsby saw that the blocks of the sidewalks really formed a ladder
盖茨比的眼角瞥见，人行道上一块块石板分明接成了一架梯子，
and mounted to a secret place above the trees—he could climb to it, if he climbed alone,
一直通向树梢上方一处隐秘的地方。他可以爬上去，只要他独自一人。
and once there he could suck on the pap of life, gulp down the incomparable milk of wonder.
到了那里，他便能吮吸生命的乳房，大口吞下那无可比拟的、令人惊叹的甘乳。
His heart beat faster as Daisy’s white face came up to his own.
黛西白皙的脸凑向他的脸，他的心跳快了起来。
He knew that when he kissed this girl, and forever wed his unutterable visions to her perishable breath,
他知道，一旦吻了这个姑娘，让那些说不出口的幻梦与她终将消逝的气息永结为一，
his mind would never romp again like the mind of God.
他的心灵就再也不能像上帝的心灵那样自由嬉游了。
So he waited, listening for a moment longer to the tuning-fork that had been struck upon a star.
于是他等了一等，又听了片刻那仿佛敲在星辰上的音叉的余音。
Then he kissed her.
然后，他吻了她。
At his lips’ touch she blossomed for him like a flower and the incarnation was complete.
他的嘴唇一碰，她便像一朵花为他绽开；他的梦终于有了血肉。
Through all he said, even through his appalling sentimentality, I was reminded of something—
听着他这番话，甚至听着他那叫人受不了的多愁善感，我依稀想起了什么——
an elusive rhythm, a fragment of lost words, that I had heard somewhere a long time ago.
一段捉摸不定的节奏，几句早已忘却的话，很久以前，我仿佛在哪里听过。
For a moment a phrase tried to take shape in my mouth and my lips parted like a dumb man’s,
有那么一会儿，一句话似乎要在我嘴边成形。我像个哑巴似的张开嘴，
as though there was more struggling upon them than a wisp of startled air.
仿佛唇间苦苦挣扎的，不只是一缕受了惊的气息。
But they made no sound, and what I had almost remembered was uncommunicable forever.
可我的嘴唇没发出一点声音，那件我几乎就要记起的事，终究再也无从说起。
